entry.title: Off-Policy RL for LLMs, Explained Visually
entry.content:
Part 1 derived the policy gradient for language models. A cartoon of on-policy training. The sampler is the trainer, so training heads straight for high reward. It ended by describing the on-policy assumption, which says that the model generating the completions is the exact one we differentiate during training. That assumption rarely holds in practice. This post covers what happens when training goes off-policy and the two main ways to correct for it, importance sampling and score centering.

Recap

Part 1 ended by looking at the policy gradient one token at a time. At a given position in the completion, each possible next token vvv has a probability pvp_vpv​ and a score sv=∇θlog⁡pvs_v = \nabla_\theta \log p_vsv​=∇θ​logpv​. The sampled token yty_tyt​ contributes R sytR \, s_{y_t}Rsyt​​ to the policy gradient, where RRR is the completion’s reward.

The key fact from part 1 is that the score has zero mean when the token is sampled from ppp:

Eyt∼p[syt]=∑vpv ∇θlog⁡pv=∇θ∑vpv=0 \mathbb{E}_{y_t \sim p}[s_{y_t}] = \sum_v p_v \, \nabla_\theta \log p_v = \nabla_\theta \sum_v p_v = 0 Eyt​∼p​[syt​​]=v∑​pv​∇θ​logpv​=∇θ​v∑​pv​=0

The same fact is why subtracting a baseline bbb from the reward doesn’t change the expected gradient, since b sytb \, s_{y_t}bsyt​​ averages to zero as well. Off-policy, the score no longer averages to zero, so both properties break.

The examples in this post reuse the prompt from part 1, “What is 17 × 24?”. The running example from part 1. After “17 × 24 = 17 × 20 + 17 × 4 = 340 +”, the model gives the correct next token, 68, a probability of 0.82, and the slip 58 a probability of 0.07. Choosing 68 leads to the right answer (408) and reward 1, while the slip 58 leads to a wrong answer and reward 0.

Where off-policy data comes from

Training is off-policy whenever the completions come from a distribution qqq other than the policy pθp_\thetapθ​ being updated. In LLM RL, an inference engine generates the rollouts and a training framework updates the weights, so we’ll call qqq the sampler and pθp_\thetapθ​ the trainer. Any gap between the two is called the training-inference mismatch. It is famously hard to get rid of, and it can quietly degrade training or collapse the reward entirely.Supervised fine-tuning, by contrast, happily trains on text generated by an entirely different model or written by a person, with no correction at all.

There are three common causes of unwanted mismatch. Two come from timing, because the sampler generated the rollouts using older weights than the trainer’s current ones. The third comes from computation, because the two engines compute slightly different probabilities even from the same weights.

Multiple updates per batch

Generating rollouts is often the most expensive part of RL for LLMs, so trainers usually split each batch of rollouts into minibatches and take one gradient step on each. DAPO, for example, splits each batch into 16 steps. Only the first step is on-policy. After that first step, θ\thetaθ has moved, and every later minibatch comes from a slightly older policy.Classic PPO goes further and makes several passes, or epochs, over the same batch. Recent LLM recipes mostly avoid this for stability. TRL’s GRPO trainer, for example, defaults to a single pass. This staleness is a deliberate tradeoff for sample efficiency, and proximal policy optimization (PPO) introduced ratio clipping specifically to handle it.

Stale weights

To keep GPUs busy, large-scale RL runs inference and training asynchronously and serves rollouts with continuous batching. While the sampler is still generating a slow rollout, the trainer keeps updating the weights on faster ones that already finished. By the time that rollout completes, the trainer has moved on to a newer checkpoint, and if new weights sync mid-generation, a single rollout can even span several checkpoints. This staleness is worst in long agentic tasks, where some episodes finish in minutes and others take hours or days.

Numerical differences

Even with fresh weights and a single gradient step, the sampler and trainer rarely compute the exact same probabilities. They are usually different programs: after the sampler generates a rollout, the trainer runs its own forward pass over those tokens to compute log-probabilities for the policy gradient loss. Even on identical weights, the two forward passes can disagree for two reasons:

  • Different precisions and codebases. The two engines may run at different precisions, such as an fp8 or int8 sampler paired with a bf16 trainer, or a quantized KV cache.A floating-point format can store only a fixed number of values between consecutive powers of two, and every weight and activation is rounded to the nearest one. bf16 has 128 values between 1 and 2, spaced 1/1281/1281/128 apart, while fp8’s e4m3 format has only 8, spaced 1/81/81/8 apart. So the same weight, 1.3, is stored as 1.296875 in bf16 but 1.25 in fp8. They may also come from independent codebases, each with its own hard-to-detect bugs.
  • Same kernels, different shapes. Even with identical, correct kernels, the sampler decodes one token at a time while the trainer scores the whole completion in one forward pass. Different input shapes can change the order of floating-point reductions, and floating-point addition isn’t associative.Addition is associative when (a+b)+c(a + b) + c(a+b)+c always equals a+(b+c)a + (b + c)a+(b+c). Floating-point addition isn’t, because each intermediate sum is rounded to the nearest representable number, and representable numbers get sparser as they grow. In bf16, they are 1 apart just below 256 but 2 apart above it, so 257 has no exact representation and rounds back to 256. So (1+1)+256=258(1 + 1) + 256 = 258(1+1)+256=258, but 1+(1+256)1 + (1 + 256)1+(1+256) rounds to 256256256 at each step. When different kernels add a long sum of logits or attention scores in a different order, the final result can differ slightly for the same reason. Batch-invariant kernels remove the dependence on shape, but they take real engineering effort and cost GPU utilization. Running both engines in fp16 instead of bf16 greatly reduces the mismatch, but doesn’t eliminate it.

At the “340 +” slot from part 1, for example, the two engines can disagree slightly about the next token, even with identical weights:

Here the trainer gives the slip 58 a probability of 0.07, while the sampler used 0.06. Small discrepancies like this show up at every token of every rollout.

Small as they are, these differences can build up over training and grow larger in long responses, where the reward signal is already thin (a fixed number of bits of feedback spread across more tokens) and asynchronous execution adds staleness on top.

All three sources of mismatch come from deliberate throughput tradeoffs. Multiple updates per batch, asynchronous rollouts, and fast inference kernels make RL practical at scale, and giving them up would make training much slower. So the practical question is how to train well on off-policy data.

Sampling from a better model

In all three cases above, the sampler is meant to be a copy of the trainer, so any gap between them is error. Other times, the data comes from a different source on purpose, because it can show the trainer something it wouldn’t produce on its own:

  • A stronger model. Rollouts from a larger or better model can show the trainer solutions it would rarely find on its own. LUFFY, for example, mixes reasoning traces from a stronger model into on-policy RL.
  • A teacher with extra context. Even the same model can act as a teacher if its prompt includes the reference solution or other privileged information; the student then learns from those completions without seeing the hint. STaR’s rationalization step works this way, giving the correct answer as a hint. Instead of generating completions, the teacher can also score the student’s rollouts.
  • People. Hand-written demonstrations are the oldest kind of off-policy data, and SFT trains on them with no correction at all.

Here the gap between sampler and trainer carries useful signal rather than error, and the question is how much of it the trainer should absorb. The gap can also be large, which weakens corrections that assume a small mismatch. The rest of this post focuses on unwanted mismatch.

Why off-policy updates go wrong

The policy gradient is an expectation over completions from the policy being trained. With off-policy data, the REINFORCE estimator averages the same quantity over the sampler’s completions instead. The trainer computes the same formula on each completion, R(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)R(y) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)R(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y), but averaging it over qqq instead of pθp_\thetapθ​ changes the expectation:

Ey∼q[R(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)]≠Ey∼pθ[R(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)]=∇θJ(θ) \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}\big[R(y) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)\big] \\ &\quad \neq \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_\theta}\big[R(y) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)\big] = \nabla_\theta J(\theta) \end{aligned} ​Ey∼q​[R(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y)]=Ey∼pθ​​[R(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y)]=∇θ​J(θ)​

To see what goes wrong, look at a single token position under a constant reward.

A thought experiment: constant reward

Suppose every completion earns the same reward, R=1R = 1R=1, no matter what it says. There is nothing to learn, and on-policy the expected update is exactly zero. At each position, the sampled token’s score averages to Ep[syt]=0\mathbb{E}_p[s_{y_t}] = 0Ep​[syt​​]=0, so Ep[R syt]=R⋅0\mathbb{E}_p[R \, s_{y_t}] = R \cdot 0Ep​[Rsyt​​]=R⋅0.

Off-policy, the sampler qqq draws the token, while the trainer ppp still computes its score. The average score is then

sˉ=Eyt∼q[syt]=∑vqv ∇θlog⁡pv, \bar{s} = \mathbb{E}_{y_t \sim q}[s_{y_t}] = \sum_v q_v \, \nabla_\theta \log p_v , sˉ=Eyt​∼q​[syt​​]=v∑​qv​∇θ​logpv​,

and the zero-mean identity no longer applies, because the weights qvq_vqv​ are not the probabilities pvp_vpv​ inside the score. In general sˉ≠0\bar{s} \neq 0sˉ=0, so the expected update Eq[R syt]=R sˉ\mathbb{E}_q[R \, s_{y_t}] = R \, \bar{s}Eq​[Rsyt​​]=Rsˉ isn’t zero either. The model moves even though the reward carries no information.

That update points along sˉ\bar{s}sˉ, which is the negative gradient of the cross-entropy loss −∑vqvlog⁡pv-\sum_v q_v \log p_v−∑v​qv​logpv​ between qqq and ppp. Minimizing that loss trains ppp to imitate qqq, so with a constant reward, off-policy policy gradient is supervised distillation of the trainer toward the sampler. It pulls ppp toward whatever qqq does, including every quirk of its numerics or staleness.

Drift and signal

When the reward varies across completions, the covariance identity E[AB]=E[A] E[B]+Cov(A,B)\mathbb{E}[AB] = \mathbb{E}[A]\,\mathbb{E}[B] + \mathrm{Cov}(A, B)E[AB]=E[A]E[B]+Cov(A,B) splits the update into a part from the mismatch and a part from the reward. As before, fix the prompt and the prefix before position ttt. Averaging over the next token yt∼qy_t \sim qyt​∼q and the rest of the completion (which determines RRR) gives:

Eq[R syt]⏟policy gradient update=Eq[R]  sˉ⏟drift+Covq(R,  syt)⏟signal \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[R \, s_{y_t}]}_{\text{policy gradient update}} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[R] \; \bar{s}}_{\text{drift}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Cov}_q(R, \; s_{y_t})}_{\text{signal}} policy gradient updateEq​[Rsyt​​]​​=driftEq​[R]sˉ​​+signalCovq​(R,syt​​)​​

  • The signal term is the only one that depends on which tokens led to which rewards. It is large when tokens that tend to produce high reward have scores pointing in a consistent direction. This is the part of the update we actually want.
  • The drift term depends on the rewards only through their average. Its direction is sˉ\bar{s}sˉ, the distillation direction from the thought experiment, scaled by how much reward the prefix typically earns.

On-policy, q=pq = pq=p, so sˉ=0\bar{s} = 0sˉ=0 and the drift term vanishes. It exists only because of the mismatch.

Why drift compounds

Distilling toward a sampler that never changes is benign. A frozen sampler: training settles short of the peak. Its target stays put, so ppp simply converges toward qqq and stops. But in RL for language models, the sampler doesn’t stay fixed. Every weight sync refreshes it from the trainer’s latest weights, and it then adds its own numerical bias on top. So the sampler is a slightly biased copy of the trainer that moves whenever the trainer does.

That closes a feedback loop. A synced sampler: the reward peaks, then falls. Each step pulls the trainer toward the biased sampler, and the next sync copies those new weights back into the sampler, which applies its bias again. If that bias points the same way from one step to the next, each pull adds to the last and the error keeps growing. A quantized sampler could produce this kind of persistent bias: its rounding error is a deterministic function of the weights, and the weights change only a little per step (though nothing guarantees that successive pulls line up).We don’t yet know whether real numerical bias persists across steps. The trainer–sampler gap has been seen to grow during training, but kernel errors also look like symmetric noise, which would partly cancel. That may explain why off-policy runs often look fine for a while and then suddenly collapse.

At scale, Modal saw this pattern training a 35B model on agentic coding. In every run that collapsed, the sampler–trainer KL had first grown threefold or more. Samplers matched to the trainer’s hardware and precision started with about a quarter of the mismatch, but GRPO still collapsed on them, just later. With the corrections below, runs stayed stable at nearly five times the mismatch. So the mismatch’s growth predicted collapse, and its starting size didn’t.

Evidence: frozen vs synced samplers

This feedback loop makes a testable prediction. With a frozen sampler, training with +1/0+1/0+1/0 rewards is ordinary SFT on the correct completions, which is stable even on text from a completely different model. With a synced sampler, the same rewards should become unstable, because the sampler is a biased copy of the trainer that keeps getting refreshed.

Marek and Ryabinin test this by training Qwen3-1.7B on the Countdown arithmetic game, with the sampler’s weights slightly perturbed to create a controlled mismatch. They compare three reward schemes, +1/0+1/0+1/0, +1/−1+1/{-}1+1/−1, and group-centered, with the sampler either frozen (never updated) or synced from the trainer after every step.Redrawn from Marek and Ryabinin (2026), Figure 2. Each curve is the mean of three seeds.

  • With a frozen sampler, only +1/0+1/0+1/0 is stable, since it reduces to SFT on the correct completions. The two schemes with negative rewards collapse within 20 steps for a different reason: pushing down the probability of fixed bad completions has no floor, as log⁡p\log plogp can fall to −∞-\infty−∞.
  • With a synced sampler, the ordering flips. +1/0+1/0+1/0, the SFT-like setting, collapses first, +1/−1+1/{-}1+1/−1 lasts longer, and group-centered rewards stay stable.

The drift term explains the ordering with a synced sampler. Its size is set by the average reward E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R], and at the same accuracy, the three schemes give very different averages:

  • With +1/0+1/0+1/0 rewards, E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R] equals the accuracy, about 0.5 to 0.6 in these runs, so the drift is large from the first step. This run collapses first.
  • With +1/−1+1/{-}1+1/−1 rewards, E[R]=2⋅accuracy−1\mathbb{E}[R] = 2 \cdot \text{accuracy} - 1E[R]=2⋅accuracy−1. At the starting accuracy of about 45%, that’s close to zero, and it reaches only about 0.4 once the model improves. The drift is smaller, and this run lasts longer before collapsing.
  • With group-centered rewards, E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R] is zero at the prompt by construction, whatever the accuracy.This holds when every completion counts equally, as in the original GRPO loss, which averages over each completion’s tokens. Variants like DAPO and Dr. GRPO weight every token equally instead, so longer completions count more. The drift shared by every token then scales with a length-weighted average advantage, ∑iAiLi/∑iLi\sum_i A_i L_i / \sum_i L_i∑i​Ai​Li​/∑i​Li​ for completions of length LiL_iLi​, which is zero only if right and wrong completions are equally long. This run stays stable.

Even when E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R] is zero across whole completions, though, it rarely stays zero at individual prefixes.

Drift survives group centering

Group centering, as in GRPO, works at the sequence level. It subtracts the group’s average reward from each completion’s reward, and every token in the completion shares that same advantage. Because those advantages average to zero across the group, you might expect the drift to vanish. At any token position, though, drift scales with the expected advantage at that prefix. That token-level average can be far from zero even when the whole group averages to zero.

A prefix that has already made the “340 + 58” slip is headed for a wrong answer, so its expected advantage is negative. A prefix that is on track, like “340 + 68”, has a positive one. These prefix-level averages are largest in magnitude where the outcome is already mostly decided. There the later tokens barely affect the reward, so the signal is near zero and the update is almost pure drift.

Group centering shrinks the drift, which explains why it is the most stable of the three schemes above, but it doesn’t eliminate it. Promising prefixes still pull the trainer toward the sampler, and mistakes push it away, even at tokens that don’t affect the reward.

Importance sampling

The classical fix for training on samples from the wrong distribution is importance sampling, a general Monte Carlo technique for estimating an expectation under one distribution using samples drawn from another.Here we use only the reweighting step, which some authors call importance weighting. Classic importance sampling also chooses the distribution to sample from, often to reduce variance. In RL the samples come from whatever sampler produced them, so there is no such choice to make. The RL literature still calls it importance sampling, and method names like TIS and MIS follow that usage.

Reweighting the samples

For any function fff, Weighted by the exact importance ratios, the sampler’s bias no longer matters. The trainer follows the on-policy path.

Ey∼p[f(y)]=∑yp(y) f(y)=∑yq(y) p(y)q(y) f(y)=Ey∼q[p(y)q(y) f(y)] \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p}[f(y)] &= \sum_y p(y) \, f(y) \\ &= \sum_y q(y) \, \frac{p(y)}{q(y)} \, f(y) \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}\Big[\frac{p(y)}{q(y)} \, f(y)\Big] \end{aligned} Ey∼p​[f(y)]​=y∑​p(y)f(y)=y∑​q(y)q(y)p(y)​f(y)=Ey∼q​[q(y)p(y)​f(y)]​

Each sample is weighted by its importance ratio p(y)/q(y)p(y)/q(y)p(y)/q(y). If the sampler generates a completion more often than the trainer would, the completion gets down-weighted, and if it generates one less often, that one gets up-weighted. On average, the samples then count as if they had been drawn from ppp. The only requirement is that the sampler can generate everything the trainer can: q(y)>0q(y) > 0q(y)>0 wherever p(y)>0p(y) > 0p(y)>0.Top-p and top-k sampling break this, because tokens outside the nucleus have q=0q = 0q=0 but p>0p > 0p>0. The usual fix, used by MAI-Thinking-1 and DeepSeek, is to apply the sampler’s mask in the trainer too, so ppp has the same support as qqq.

Applied to the policy gradient, with f(y)=R(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)f(y) = R(y) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)f(y)=R(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y), this gives an unbiased estimate from the sampler’s rollouts:

Reweighting is also cheap. The trainer already computes pθ(y)p_\theta(y)pθ​(y) in its forward pass, and inference engines can return the log-probabilities of the tokens they sample at almost no extra cost.

Why sequence-level ratios explode

A completion’s probability is the product of its token probabilities, so its importance ratio is a product of per-token ratios:

Each factor is usually close to 1,In the worked example from earlier, at “340 +” in 17 × 24, the trainer gives the slip 58 a probability of 0.07 and the sampler 0.06, so its factor is 0.07/0.06≈1.170.07 / 0.06 \approx 1.170.07/0.06≈1.17. The factor for 68 is 0.82/0.83≈0.990.82 / 0.83 \approx 0.990.82/0.83≈0.99. but a completion has hundreds or thousands of them, and small factors compound. Token-level ratios

Sequence-level importance sampling weights every token’s score in a completion by the same number, the product of all its per-token ratios. In practice, almost every method uses token-level ratios instead, weighting each token’s score by its own ratio rtr_trt​:

∑trt R syt,rt=pθ(yt∣y<t)q(yt∣y<t) \sum_t r_t \, R \, s_{y_t}, \qquad r_t = \frac{p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t})}{q(y_t \mid y_{<t})} t∑​rt​Rsyt​​,rt​=q(yt​∣y<t​)pθ​(yt​∣y<t​)​

Compared with the exact sequence ratio, this keeps one factor of the product and sets all the others to 1. Every token gets its own correction, but each term reweights only the choice of that token itself. It leaves the prefix before the token and the continuation after it (which decides the reward) uncorrected:

The token itself is corrected exactly. With its prefix held fixed, weighting the sampled token by rtr_trt​ turns an average over the sampler’s next-token distribution into an average over the trainer’s. In particular, it restores the zero-mean identity from the recap:

Eyt∼q[rt syt]=∑vqv pvqv sv=∑vpv sv=0 \mathbb{E}_{y_t \sim q}[r_t \, s_{y_t}] = \sum_v q_v \, \frac{p_v}{q_v} \, s_v = \sum_v p_v \, s_v = 0 Eyt​∼q​[rt​syt​​]=v∑​qv​qv​pv​​sv​=v∑​pv​sv​=0

So the drift term vanishes at every prefix, and only the signal is left.

The prefix and continuation in that term are not corrected. Both still come from the sampler, which decides what prefixes the token is trained on (like “340 +”) and how the completion finishes from there to earn its reward. Correcting for those would require multiplying in the ratios of every other token, which is the product that explodes. So token-level importance sampling is an approximation. It works well when the sampler and trainer are close, since they then reach similar prefixes and finish them in similar ways.

Token ratios are much better behaved than their product, but they are still unbounded. The largest ones come from tokens that the trainer finds much more likely than the sampler did. A token with q=0.001q = 0.001q=0.001 and p=0.01p = 0.01p=0.01 gets a weight of 10. Any one such token is rare, but a batch has millions of tokens, so some appear in every batch. A handful of heavily weighted tokens can then dominate the gradient. The weight never divides by zero, since the sampler produced each token and so gave it q>0q > 0q>0, but it has no ceiling.

A gradient dominated by a few tokens causes three problems. It points wherever their scores point, so it swings from batch to batch depending on which rare tokens happened to be drawn. The two engines also disagree most on those tokens, often because of numerical error, so the gradient leans hardest on its least reliable parts. And a single huge weight inflates the gradient’s norm. If gradients are clipped by norm, as they usually are, the whole update shrinks, and every other token’s contribution with it.

Bounding the ratio: TIS, MIS, and PPO

Score centering vs importance sampling

Computed exactly, both methods cancel drift, but they get there differently. Importance sampling multiplies each sampled token’s score by its own weight, which depends on which token was drawn and can be huge for rare ones; practical versions bound that weight, and bounding lets drift back in. A stale sampler runs older weights, so its offset, δ=z(θold)−z(θ)\delta = z(\theta_{\text{old}}) - z(\theta)δ=z(θold​)−z(θ), moves exactly opposite to the trainer’s logits and cancels any change to the current weights. The stale sampler doesn’t respond to the current weights at all, so it has no gradient for centering to match, and the sampler-gradient reading doesn’t apply.

Computing the expected score

For a language model, sˉ\bar{s}sˉ is a sum over the vocabulary, just like the softmax. With continuous or combinatorial actions it usually has no closed form, which is one reason off-policy methods there rely on importance sampling instead.

Even for a language model, though, sˉ\bar{s}sˉ needs the sampler’s full next-token distribution at every position, while inference engines normally return only the sampled token’s probability. Logging the whole distribution is expensive. With a 152K-token vocabulary, one position takes about 600 KB in fp32, so a batch of 1,024 rollouts of 32K tokens each would need about 20 TB!

One practical approximation logs only the sampler’s top kkk probabilities (the head HHH) and fills in the rest of the vocabulary (the tail TTT) with the trainer’s probabilities, rescaled to sum to one:Another option is a Monte Carlo estimate. At each position, have the sampler draw a few extra tokens (without continuing or grading them) and subtract their average score. That needs no tail model and is exact on average, but it adds noise, and a single estimate isn’t exactly zero even on-policy. Thinking Machines’ StableReinforce loss appears to do exactly this with 8 tokens per position, as Martin Marek found by recovering its gradients.

q^v={qvv∈Hρ pvv∈Tρ=1−∑v∈Hqv1−∑v∈Hpv \hat{q}_v = \begin{cases} q_v & v \in H \\ \rho \, p_v & v \in T \end{cases} \qquad \rho = \frac{1 - \sum_{v \in H} q_v}{1 - \sum_{v \in H} p_v} q^​v​={qv​ρpv​​v∈Hv∈T​ρ=1−∑v∈H​pv​1−∑v∈H​qv​​

The tail never has to be summed. Because the trainer’s expected score is zero, the tail’s part of it is minus the head’s part, and the correction reduces to a sum over the kkk head tokens:

Eq^[s]=∑v∈Hqv sv+ρ∑v∈Tpv sv=∑v∈Hqv sv+ρ (∑vpv sv⏟= 0−∑v∈Hpv sv)=∑v∈H(qv−ρ pv) sv \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{\hat{q}}[s] &= \sum_{v \in H} q_v \, s_v + \rho \sum_{v \in T} p_v \, s_v \\ &= \sum_{v \in H} q_v \, s_v + \rho \, \Big( \underbrace{\sum_{v} p_v \, s_v}_{=\,0} - \sum_{v \in H} p_v \, s_v \Big) \\ &= \sum_{v \in H} \big( q_v - \rho \, p_v \big) \, s_v \end{aligned} Eq^​​[s]​=v∈H∑​qv​sv​+ρv∈T∑​pv​sv​=v∈H∑​qv​sv​+ρ(=0v∑​pv​sv​​​−v∈H∑​pv​sv​)=v∈H∑​(qv​−ρpv​)sv​​

This is exact on the head and biased only through the tail model. Next-token distributions are concentrated enough that the tail barely matters.With k=128k = 128k=128, the head held more than 99.9% of the sampler’s probability on average, in all but the most aggressively quantized of Marek and Ryabinin’s settings. k=32k = 32k=32 already matched full score centering in every setting they tested, and runs with k=128k = 128k=128 finished within 1% of the baseline’s wall-clock time on their own JAX sampler. They did not measure the overhead in vLLM or SGLang.

As Modal points out, top-p sampling makes this exact. The sampler’s probabilities are zero outside its candidate set, so logging each candidate’s ID and probability (about 8 bytes each) gives sˉ\bar{s}sˉ with no tail to estimate, as long as the trainer applies the same mask to its own probabilities. The same log serves as the mask. It’s usually about the size of a top-kkk log, but it has no fixed size, since the candidate set grows wherever the sampler is uncertain.

In PyTorch, the whole loss is a few lines on top of the usual policy gradient loss. It needs the sampler’s top-kkk log-probabilities and token ids, which vLLM and SGLang can return alongside each sampled token:These must be the sampler’s final sampling probabilities, after temperature, top-p, and any other processing, and the trainer’s ppp should use the same temperature. Inference engines don’t always return that by default. vLLM, for example, returns raw log-probabilities unless logprobs_mode is set to a processed mode, and returns at most 20 per token unless max_logprobs is raised.

import torch

def score_centering_loss(train_logp, samp_topk_logp, topk_ids, sampled_ids, advantages, eps=1e-6):
    """
    train_logp:     [N, V] trainer log-probs (in fp32) at each of N positions
    samp_topk_logp: [N, k] sampler's top-k log-probs, logged during generation
    topk_ids:       [N, k] token ids of the sampler's top-k
    sampled_ids:    [N]    the token the sampler chose at each position
    advantages:     [N]    each completion's advantage, broadcast to its tokens
    """
    train_head_logp = train_logp.gather(-1, topk_ids)
    with torch.no_grad():  # no gradient through q or the tail's use of p
        q_head, p_head = samp_topk_logp.exp(), train_head_logp.exp()
        rho = (1 - q_head.sum(-1)).clamp_min(eps) / (1 - p_head.sum(-1)).clamp_min(eps)
        coef = q_head - rho[:, None] * p_head  # q_v - rho * p_v on the head
    sampled_logp = train_logp.gather(-1, sampled_ids[:, None]).squeeze(-1)
    centering = (coef * train_head_logp).sum(-1)
    return -(advantages * (sampled_logp - centering)).sum()  # normalize as your trainer does

Without the centering term, this is the ordinary policy gradient loss. The reference implementation, in JAX and PyTorch, also supports composing with TIS and MIS.

When it helps

The previous sections make two predictions. If the mismatch acts like a fixed bias, as a quantized sampler’s might, most of the damage is drift, so removing it should be enough. If the sampler is stale, centering still leaves a gap between Covq\mathrm{Cov}_qCovq​ and Covp\mathrm{Cov}_pCovp​, so it may need importance weights alongside it. Two sets of experiments bear out both. Marek and Ryabinin test each kind of mismatch on its own and make it severe on purpose, so that the methods separate within a few hundred steps. Modal trains a larger model on a realistic mix of both.

In Marek and Ryabinin’s experiments:

  • Quantized sampler.Quantizing the sampler is attractive in the first place because generating rollouts is usually the most expensive part of RL for LLMs. Lower-precision weights and KV cache make each decoding step faster and let the same GPUs hold more rollouts at once. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, vanilla policy gradient collapses once the KV cache is quantized, while score centering stays stable. At the most aggressive setting, with INT8 weights and an INT4 KV cache, score centering is the only method that trains well. TIS improves slowly and ends far behind, and everything else makes no progress, including PPO and DAPO, whose clip was designed for policy movement rather than numerical error.
  • Stale sampler. When the sampler syncs only every 64 steps, neither correction works alone. TIS collapses, and score centering oscillates. Combined, they do best, ahead of PPO and DAPO, which were built for exactly this kind of staleness.

Modal’s run points the same way. They trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on agentic coding, fully asynchronously, with samplers on six kinds of accelerators at NVFP4, FP8, and BF16, so the mismatch mixed numerical error with staleness. Score centering alone and MIS alone each delayed the collapse but didn’t prevent it, and score centering’s run collapsed after its sampler–trainer KL had grown about threefold. Only the two combined trained stably to the end, centering the masked weights the way the next section centers capped ones.

It isn’t settled why score centering alone oscillates with a stale sampler, but its logit gradient suggests a mechanism. A stale sampler with score centering alone: the trainer overshoots the peak and bounces across it. Centering’s push on each logit is set entirely by the sampler, and a stale sampler doesn’t know the trainer has moved. At “340 +”, if only 68 leads to a correct answer, a trainer that has already reached p68=0.95p_{68} = 0.95p68​=0.95 would get an on-policy push of p68(1−p68)≈0.05p_{68}(1 - p_{68}) \approx 0.05p68​(1−p68​)≈0.05 on its logit. A sampler still at q68=0.80q_{68} = 0.80q68​=0.80 makes centering push by q68(1−q68)=0.16q_{68}(1 - q_{68}) = 0.16q68​(1−q68​)=0.16, more than three times as hard. Between syncs, the trainer takes 64 steps computed for where it used to be, which acts much like one step 64 times as large. A step that large may overshoot the optimum, and the next sync may swing the trainer back past it, though as far as we know that hasn’t been tested.

Centering also removes vanilla policy gradient’s accidental KL term, which pulls the trainer toward the sampler on prefixes with positive expected reward and pushes it away on prefixes with negative expected reward. With a biased sampler, that pull is toward the bias. With a stale sampler, it is toward the trainer’s own recent weights, acting like PPO’s KL trust region. StableReinforce keeps centering but puts a small pull back on purpose, a KL term toward the sampler with a fixed weight of 0.01, in place of vanilla’s VqV_qVq​. When the sampler is a stronger model or a teacher, that pull is how the trainer imitates it, so centering removes the imitation along with the drift and learns only from the rewards.

Centered importance sampling

Score centering and importance sampling fix different parts of the update, so they can be used together. Recall the split into drift and signal:

  • Importance weights change the signal. They change how much each draw counts. With exact weights, the next token is weighted by the trainer’s probabilities instead of the sampler’s, although the prefix and the rest of the completion still come from the sampler. Bounding the weights spoils this slightly, and also lets some drift back in.
  • Centering changes only the drift. It subtracts one fixed vector per prefix, the same for every draw. That makes the weighted score average to zero at every prefix, and leaves the signal untouched, since subtracting a constant doesn’t change a covariance.

So stacking them keeps the importance-weighted signal and gets centering’s zero drift. Centering removes the drift that TIS leaves behind. In this cartoon, the capped weights still move where the signal is measured, partway from the sampler back toward the trainer, so both end up close to the peak.

Centering the weighted score

Centering works the same way here: take whatever multiplies RRR in the update and subtract its average over the sampler’s draws. In plain policy gradient that’s the score sss, whose average is sˉ\bar{s}sˉ. With TIS or MIS, it’s the weighted score w sw \, sws, so the combined update subtracts the average of the weighted score instead:

R (wyt syt−Eq[w s]),Eq[w s]=∑vqv wv sv R \, \big( w_{y_t} \, s_{y_t} - \mathbb{E}_q[w \, s] \big), \quad \mathbb{E}_q[w \, s] = \sum_v q_v \, w_v \, s_v R(wyt​​syt​​−Eq​[ws]),Eq​[ws]=v∑​qv​wv​sv​

Subtracting the plain sˉ\bar{s}sˉ here would overcorrect, since the weights have already removed most of the drift. Bounding leaves some drift behind, and this term subtracts exactly that. Computing it needs the bounded weight wvw_vwv​, such as min⁡(pv/qv,2)\min(p_v / q_v, 2)min(pv​/qv​,2), for every token in the vocabulary, not just the sampled one.The top-kkk approximation still works. On the modeled tail, every token’s ratio is pv/q^v=1/ρp_v / \hat{q}_v = 1/\rhopv​/q^​v​=1/ρ, so they all get the same weight f(1/ρ)f(1/\rho)f(1/ρ), and the average weighted score is again a sum over the head: Eq^[w s]=∑v∈H(qv wv−ρ f(1/ρ) pv) sv\mathbb{E}_{\hat{q}}[w \, s] = \sum_{v \in H} \big( q_v \, w_v - \rho \, f(1/\rho) \, p_v \big) \, s_vEq^​​[ws]=∑v∈H​(qv​wv​−ρf(1/ρ)pv​)sv​. With w=1w = 1w=1, this is the plain correction above.

In the figure below, TIS alone leaves a small nonzero average (the leftover drift). Subtracting that same vector from every draw moves the average to zero while keeping the differences between draws, which carry the signal, unchanged.

Two special cases confirm the formula. With w=1w = 1w=1, this is plain score centering. With exact token-level weights, w=p/qw = p / qw=p/q, the subtracted term is ∑vpv sv=0\sum_v p_v \, s_v = 0∑v​pv​sv​=0, and there’s nothing left to center.

The same holds for whole rollouts. With exact, unclipped sequence-level importance weights, the update already equals the trainer’s gradient in expectation, because the weights correct the prefixes and the rest of the completion as well as each token. Score centering would add nothing there.Han and Hu frame both corrections as estimates of Cov(R,w s)\mathrm{Cov}(R, w\,s)Cov(R,ws). Unlike the policy gradient under capped or masked weights, the covariance ignores a constant added to the reward. A group baseline estimates it by centering the reward, and score centering by centering the weighted score. With sequence-level weights the baseline is enough, but with token-level weights it generally leaves a bias that centering removes. But those weights’ variance explodes with length, so every practical method truncates or bounds them, and the bounding brings back drift for centering to remove.

Fixing a stale sampler

In the stale-sampler experiment, centering alone oscillated, while combining it with TIS did best. With importance weights, the push depends on where the trainer is again, so it slows down near the peak and settles. Centering alone pushes each logit by R (1yt−q)R \, (\mathbf{1}_{y_t} - q)R(1yt​​−q), which is set entirely by the stale sampler. Importance weights put the trainer’s probabilities back into the update. For tokens whose ratio stays below the cap, the weight pa/qap_a / q_apa​/qa​ undoes how often the sampler picks them, turning centering’s expected logit gradient ∑aqa Qq(a) (1a−q)\sum_a q_a \, Q_q(a) \, (\mathbf{1}_a - q)∑a​qa​Qq​(a)(1a​−q) into the on-policy form ∑apa Qq(a) (1a−p)\sum_a p_a \, Q_q(a) \, (\mathbf{1}_a - p)∑a​pa​Qq​(a)(1a​−p). It isn’t the full on-policy gradient, since the rest of each completion still comes from the stale sampler. But like the on-policy push, it fades as the trainer learns a token, even while the sampler stays where it was at the last sync. That may be why the combination is stable where centering alone is not.

We don’t yet know whether these gains hold for long agentic rollouts under the milder mismatch of a well-engineered system.

Wrapping up

Everything in this post follows from one fact in part 1: the score averages to zero only when the model being trained draws the tokens. Off-policy, it averages to sˉ\bar{s}sˉ, and the policy gradient picks up a pull toward the sampler. Importance sampling removes that pull by reweighting each draw as if the trainer had made it, and score centering removes it by subtracting sˉ\bar{s}sˉ directly. Score centering alone works well when the gap behaves like a fixed bias. When the sampler is stale, though, its signal is out of date, and adding importance weights on top of centering helps by reweighting the signal toward the current trainer.

entry.title: Policy Gradient for LLMs, Explained Visually
entry.content:
Most RL algorithms used to train language models, from PPO to GRPO, are elaborations of one idea: the policy gradient. This post derives it from scratch for an LLM solving a problem with a checkable answer. It follows one prompt, “What is 17 × 24?”, from next-token probabilities to the gradient that makes correct answers more likely.

Language models as policies

Given a prompt xxx, a language model generates a completion y=(y1,…,yT)y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)y=(y1​,…,yT​) one token at a time. In RL terms, the model is a policy: at each step it looks at the prefix it has produced so far and outputs a distribution over the next token, from which one token is sampled.

The probability of the full completion is the product of the per-token probabilities:θ\thetaθ is the model’s parameters: its weights, which training adjusts.

pθ(y∣x)=∏t=1Tpθ(yt∣x,y<t) p_\theta(y \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) pθ​(y∣x)=t=1∏T​pθ​(yt​∣x,y<t​)

Generating a completion traces one path through a tree of possible continuations.Each p(⋅)p(\cdot)p(⋅) in the tree is conditioned on the prompt and on every token before it on the path, so p(24)p(24)p(24) means p(24∣x,17,×)p(24 \mid x, 17, \times)p(24∣x,17,×). The slot from the previous figure is one branch point: 68 leads to the correct answer, and the 58 slip to a wrong one. Once the model emits a stop token, a reward function grades the finished completion.

For reasoning tasks, the reward function is often a verifier that returns R(x,y)=1R(x, y) = 1R(x,y)=1 if the final answer is correct and 000 otherwise.This setup is often called RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Math problems with a known answer and coding tasks with unit tests are common examples. Our goal is to find the parameters θ\thetaθ that maximize the expected reward, which we call the objective J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ):Read the objective as: draw a prompt xxx from the training set D\mathcal{D}D, let the model generate a completion yyy, compute its reward, and average over many such draws. The letter JJJ comes from optimal control, where it names a cost to minimize. RL borrowed it for a reward to maximize, which is why it isn’t LLL, the usual letter for a loss.

J(θ)=Ex∼D,  y∼pθ(⋅∣x)[R(x,y)] J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}, \; y \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}\big[R(x, y)\big] J(θ)=Ex∼D,y∼pθ​(⋅∣x)​[R(x,y)]

This is the standard reinforcement learning objective.In general RL, an agent collects a reward after each of many actions, and the objective is the expected total reward over an episode, often discounted. Generating a completion is an episode where each token is an action and the only reward comes at the end, so the total is just R(x,y)R(x, y)R(x,y).

From here on, I’ll drop the prompt xxx from the notation; everything is conditioned on it.

The policy gradient

To improve the model, we want to follow the gradient of the objective, ∇θJ(θ)\nabla_\theta J(\theta)∇θ​J(θ): the direction in parameter space that most increases the expected reward. This gradient is the policy gradient,The name is short for the gradient of expected reward with respect to the policy’s parameters. It contrasts with value-based methods like Q-learning, which learn how good each action is and act on those estimates instead of adjusting the policy directly. The term became standard with Sutton et al. (2000). and methods that train by estimating and following it are called policy gradient methods. REINFORCE, PPO, and GRPO are all examples. They share this expected-reward goal, but PPO and GRPO also change the update itself, clipping or reweighting it to keep training stable.

The hard part is computing it. Written out, the objective is a sum over every possible completion:

J(θ)=∑ypθ(y) R(y) J(\theta) = \sum_y p_\theta(y) \, R(y) J(θ)=y∑​pθ​(y)R(y)

θ\thetaθ appears only in pθ(y)p_\theta(y)pθ​(y), how likely each completion is, and not in the reward R(y)R(y)R(y). If we could evaluate this sum, we could differentiate it directly, but there are far too many completions to enumerate.With a vocabulary of about 150,000 tokens, even a 100-token completion has more than 1050010^{500}10500 possibilities.

The usual fix for an expectation we can’t enumerate is to estimate it by sampling: generate NNN completions, compute their rewards, and average them. That gives a fine estimate of JJJ, but not one we can differentiate. The completions are discrete token sequences,At each step, the model’s probabilities define a categorical distribution over the vocabulary, and we draw one token from it. The result is an integer token ID: a small change to θ\thetaθ either leaves it unchanged or flips it, so there is no smooth gradient. (Sampling often reshapes the distribution with a temperature or top-p cutoff. The derivations here assume we sample from the model’s probabilities as-is.) and their rewards come from a verifier, a unit test, or a person, none of which we can backpropagate through. There is no path for autograd to follow from the reward back to θ\thetaθ.

Compare supervised fine-tuning, where the completion yyy is fixed training data and θ\thetaθ appears directly in the loss −log⁡pθ(y)-\log p_\theta(y)−logpθ​(y). Here, θ\thetaθ decides which completions we get, not how any one of them is graded. What we need is a way to rewrite ∇θJ\nabla_\theta J∇θ​J as an average, over sampled completions, of something we can differentiate.

The log-derivative trick

The workaround is a one-line identity, ∇θpθ=pθ∇θlog⁡pθ\nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta∇θ​pθ​=pθ​∇θ​logpθ​,By the chain rule, ∇θlog⁡pθ=∇θpθ/pθ\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta = \nabla_\theta p_\theta / p_\theta∇θ​logpθ​=∇θ​pθ​/pθ​. Multiply both sides by pθp_\thetapθ​. which moves the gradient inside the expectation:

∇θJ(θ)=∇θ Ey∼pθ[R(y)]=∇θ∑ypθ(y) R(y)=∑y∇θpθ(y)⏟depends on θ R(y)=∑ypθ(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)⏟the identity R(y)=Ey∼pθ[R(y) ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)⏟the score] \begin{aligned} \nabla_\theta J(\theta) &= \nabla_\theta \, \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_\theta}\big[R(y)\big] \\ &= \nabla_\theta \sum_y p_\theta(y) \, R(y) \\ &= \sum_y \underbrace{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(y)}_{\mathclap{\text{depends on } \theta}} \, R(y) \\ &= \sum_y \underbrace{p_\theta(y) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)}_{\mathclap{\text{the identity}}} \, R(y) \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_\theta}\big[R(y) \, \underbrace{\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)}_{\mathclap{\text{the score}}}\big] \end{aligned} ∇θ​J(θ)​=∇θ​Ey∼pθ​​[R(y)]=∇θ​y∑​pθ​(y)R(y)=y∑​depends on θ∇θ​pθ​(y)​​R(y)=y∑​the identitypθ​(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y)​​R(y)=Ey∼pθ​​[R(y)the score∇θ​logpθ​(y)​​]​

This derivation is a special case of the policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al., 2000),In general form, ∇θJ∝∑sdπ(s)∑aQπ(s,a) ∇θπθ(a∣s)\nabla_\theta J \propto \sum_s d^\pi(s) \sum_a Q^\pi(s, a)\, \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a \mid s)∇θ​J∝∑s​dπ(s)∑a​Qπ(s,a)∇θ​πθ​(a∣s), where πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ is the usual RL notation for the policy pθp_\thetapθ​, dπ(s)d^\pi(s)dπ(s) is how often it visits state sss, and Qπ(s,a)Q^\pi(s, a)Qπ(s,a) is the expected future reward after taking action aaa in state sss. (In episodic tasks, the two sides differ by a constant, which only rescales the step.) For a completion, the state is the prefix and the action is the next token. With only a final reward, QπQ^\piQπ is the expected reward of finishing from that prefix, and the sampled RRR is a one-sample estimate of it. and the third line is its key step. In general RL, a policy’s actions change which states it ends up in, so you might expect the gradient of the objective to include a term for how the distribution of visited states changes with θ\thetaθ. That term would be hard to compute, because it depends on the environment’s dynamics. The point of the theorem is that it never appears: the gradient needs only the gradients of the policy’s own probabilities, weighted by how much reward each choice leads to. For language models, this is easy to see. Appending a token always produces the same next prefix, so there are no environment dynamics, and the only way θ\thetaθ affects which completions we get is through pθp_\thetapθ​ itself.

The quantity ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)∇θ​logpθ​(y) is called the score.Don’t read much into the word: it doesn’t rate how good a completion is. The name comes from statistics, where ∇θlog⁡p\nabla_\theta \log p∇θ​logp is the score function of maximum-likelihood estimation. REINFORCE is sometimes called the score-function estimator for the same reason. It points in the direction in parameter space that most increases the log-probability of the completion yyy. The final line is an expectation over completions sampled from the policy pθp_\thetapθ​ itself, so we can estimate it by sampling. Perform NNN rollouts (that is, draw NNN completions from the policy), score each one, and average:

∇θJ(θ)≈1N∑i=1NR(yi) ∇θlog⁡pθ(yi),yi∼pθ \nabla_\theta J(\theta) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} R(y_i) \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y_i), \qquad y_i \sim p_\theta ∇θ​J(θ)≈N1​i=1∑N​R(yi​)∇θ​logpθ​(yi​),yi​∼pθ​

This is the REINFORCE estimator,Introduced by Ronald Williams in Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning (1992). PPO, GRPO, DAPO, and most other RL algorithms used for LLMs today are elaborations of this estimator. also known as the Monte Carlo policy gradient: it estimates the gradient by averaging over complete sampled rollouts, using each one’s actual reward rather than a learned estimate of how good it was.It is unbiased: averaged over many batches, it equals the true gradient. Any single batch, though, can point well away from it. Each term pairs a direction with a weight: the score points toward making that rollout’s completion more likely, and the reward sets how much that direction counts.

Because all completions share a total probability of 1, B’s and C’s gains come from elsewhere, here mostly from completions nobody sampled. A barely changes, because it shares everything up to “340 +” with B, so reinforcing B also lifts most of A’s path. The numbers are only illustrative: B and C are pushed up, but how every other completion moves depends on how the model’s parameters are shared.

With the reward held fixed, R ∇θlog⁡pθ(y)R \, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y)R∇θ​logpθ​(y) is exactly the gradient of Rlog⁡pθ(y)R \log p_\theta(y)Rlogpθ​(y): a log-likelihood on one of the model’s own samples, weighted by its reward. So policy gradient is supervised fine-tuning on your own samples, weighted by reward. With +1/0+1/0+1/0 rewards, as in the figure above, it is literally SFT on the correct completions, so incorrect completions are never pushed down directly; they only lose share.Training on your own correct samples is also used on its own, as rejection-sampling fine-tuning or expert iteration. STaR is an early example for reasoning.

From sequences to tokens

A completion’s log-probability is a sum of per-token log-probabilities, so its score breaks into one term per token:

∇θlog⁡pθ(y)=∑t=1T∇θlog⁡pθ(yt∣y<t) \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t}) ∇θ​logpθ​(y)=t=1∑T​∇θ​logpθ​(yt​∣y<t​)

Each term is the score of a single token: the direction that most increases the probability of choosing yty_tyt​, given everything generated before it. So we can study the update one position at a time. Pick a single position, such as the slot right after “340 +” in the 17 × 24 example, and hold its prefix y<ty_{<t}y<t​ fixed. For each token vvv in the vocabulary, write

pv=pθ(v∣y<t)andsv=∇θlog⁡pv p_v = p_\theta(v \mid y_{<t}) \qquad \text{and} \qquad s_v = \nabla_\theta \log p_v pv​=pθ​(v∣y<t​)andsv​=∇θ​logpv​

for the model’s probability of choosing vvv at this position and that token’s score. In the example, p68=0.82p_{68} = 0.82p68​=0.82 and p58=0.07p_{58} = 0.07p58​=0.07.

Only one token is actually sampled at each position. Its contribution to the update is R sytR \, s_{y_t}Rsyt​​: that token’s score, multiplied by the reward the whole completion earned.

To see what a token’s score looks like, look at the last layer. At one position, the network outputs a logit zuz_uzu​ for every token uuu in the vocabulary, and p=softmax⁡(z)p = \operatorname{softmax}(z)p=softmax(z). Differentiating the log-softmax gives the logit gradient of the chosen token vvv:

log⁡pv=zv−log⁡∑uezu⟹∂log⁡pv∂zu={1−pvu=v−puu≠v \log p_v = z_v - \log \sum_u e^{z_u} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial \log p_v}{\partial z_u} = \begin{cases} 1 - p_v & u = v \\ -p_u & u \neq v \end{cases} logpv​=zv​−logu∑​ezu​⟹∂zu​∂logpv​​={1−pv​−pu​​u=vu=v​

It is positive on the chosen token’s own logit, negative on every other logit in proportion to that token’s probability, and sums to zero. The score is this vector carried back through the network to the parameters by the chain rule:

sv=∑u(1[u=v]−pu) ∇θzu s_v = \sum_u \big(\mathbb{1}[u = v] - p_u\big) \, \nabla_\theta z_u sv​=u∑​(1[u=v]−pu​)∇θ​zu​

As pv→1p_v \to 1pv​→1, every coefficient in this sum goes to zero, so the score does too. Across completions A and B from the figure above:

The reward only says whether the finished completion was right, so every position gets the same RRR, whatever its token did:This is the credit assignment problem. Methods that learn a value function, or use process reward models that grade intermediate steps, try to give individual tokens their own credit. A’s correct opening steps get nothing, and B’s filler tokens get the full reward. What differs from token to token is the score, which is tiny for tokens the model was already sure of.The actual step also scales with the learning rate and depends on how the network maps parameters to logits, and a token’s probability can still change because of other tokens’ gradients.

The score has zero mean

The score has a simple but important property. On-policy, when the token is sampled from the same distribution ppp whose score we compute, the expected score is exactly zero:

Eyt∼p[syt]=∑vpv ∇θlog⁡pv=∑v∇θpv=∇θ∑vpv=∇θ1=0 \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{y_t \sim p}[s_{y_t}] &= \sum_v p_v \, \nabla_\theta \log p_v = \sum_v \nabla_\theta p_v \\ &= \nabla_\theta \sum_v p_v = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0 \end{aligned} Eyt​∼p​[syt​​]​=v∑​pv​∇θ​logpv​=v∑​∇θ​pv​=∇θ​v∑​pv​=∇θ​1=0​

Intuitively, probability is conserved. Any change to θ\thetaθ that makes some tokens more likely must make others less likely by the same total amount. Weighted by how often each token is sampled, the pushes cancel.

We can check this at the logits. In vector form, the logit gradient from the previous section is 1v−p\mathbf{1}_v - p1v​−p, where 1v\mathbf{1}_v1v​ is the one-hot vector for vvv; the zoom-ins in the figure above show it for 68 and for “=”. Averaging these vectors over which token gets sampled, weighted by ppp, gives ∑vpv(1v−p)=p−p=0\sum_v p_v (\mathbf{1}_v - p) = p - p = 0∑v​pv​(1v​−p)=p−p=0.

Baselines and group centering

Nothing so far required the rewards to be +1/0+1/0+1/0. What if we use +1/−1+1/-1+1/−1 instead? That doubles every reward and then subtracts 1. Doubling just doubles the gradient. For the shift, the zero-mean identity is the answer: we can subtract any baseline bbb from the reward without changing the expected gradient, as long as bbb does not depend on the sampled token:

Ep[(R−b) syt]=Ep[R syt]−b Ep[syt]⏟= 0=Ep[R syt] \mathbb{E}_{p}\big[(R - b) \, s_{y_t}\big] = \mathbb{E}_{p}[R \, s_{y_t}] - b \, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{p}[s_{y_t}]}_{=\,0} = \mathbb{E}_{p}[R \, s_{y_t}] Ep​[(R−b)syt​​]=Ep​[Rsyt​​]−b=0Ep​[syt​​]​​=Ep​[Rsyt​​]

The quantity A=R−bA = R - bA=R−b is called the advantage. Subtracting a baseline adds no bias: REINFORCE stays unbiased, with exactly the same expected gradient. What it can change is the variance, and a well-chosen baseline reduces it dramatically.See Greensmith, Bartlett, and Baxter (2004) for a thorough treatment of baselines as variance reduction for policy gradient estimates. To see why, split each rollout’s term in two:

R syt=b syt⏟mean zero, but noisy+(R−b) syt⏟the advantage-weighted part R \, s_{y_t} = \underbrace{b \, s_{y_t}}_{\text{mean zero, but noisy}} + \underbrace{(R - b) \, s_{y_t}}_{\text{the advantage-weighted part}} Rsyt​​=mean zero, but noisybsyt​​​​+the advantage-weighted part(R−b)syt​​​​

The first part contributes nothing to the expected gradient, but each sample of it is a large vector pointing somewhere different. In the extreme case where every completion earns R=1R = 1R=1, the true gradient is zero, yet each sample still pushes its own log-probabilities up at random. With b=1b = 1b=1, every term vanishes. How much a baseline helps depends on bbb. The standard choice is the prompt’s expected reward. It isn’t exactly optimal,The variance depends on bbb only through E[(R−b)2∥s∥2]\mathbb{E}\big[(R - b)^2 \lVert s \rVert^2\big]E[(R−b)2∥s∥2], which is minimized at b⋆=E[R∥s∥2]/E[∥s∥2]b^\star = \mathbb{E}\big[R \lVert s \rVert^2\big] / \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert s \rVert^2\big]b⋆=E[R∥s∥2]/E[∥s∥2]. This is close to E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R] only when the reward is roughly unrelated to the size of the score. They can differ a lot: for a binary choice that succeeds with probability 0.1, successes have the larger score, so b⋆=0.9b^\star = 0.9b⋆=0.9 while E[R]=0.1\mathbb{E}[R] = 0.1E[R]=0.1. but it is simple to estimate, and because some prompts are far easier than others, estimating it per prompt removes a large source of noise.

GRPOIntroduced in DeepSeekMath. GRPO also divides by the group’s reward standard deviation. Dr. GRPO argues that this normalization introduces a bias toward easy and hard prompts. Here I use mean-centering only. Because the group mean includes the completion’s own reward, the expected gradient is scaled by 1−1/G1 - 1/G1−1/G. When every prompt uses the same GGG, that is just a slightly smaller step size. A leave-one-out baseline, as in RLOO, removes the factor. popularized a simple, critic-freeA critic is a second network trained to predict the expected reward, the value V(x)V(x)V(x), to use as the baseline. PPO usually trains one alongside the policy. GRPO replaces it with the group’s mean reward, which saves a model of similar size to the policy. baseline for LLMs: sample a group of GGG completions for each prompt and use the group’s mean reward as the baseline for each of them:

Ai=Ri−1G∑j=1GRj A_i = R_i - \frac{1}{G} \sum_{j=1}^{G} R_j Ai​=Ri​−G1​j=1∑G​Rj​

Correct completions now get a positive advantage and are reinforced. Incorrect completions get a negative advantage and are suppressed. Prompts where every completion succeeds, or every completion fails, contribute nothing. For the four rollouts from earlier:

REINFORCE with group-centered advantages fits in a few lines of PyTorch:

def reinforce_loss(logprobs, rewards, mask, group_size):
    # logprobs: (B, T) per-token log p_θ(y_t | y_<t)
    # rewards:  (B,)   one per completion, grouped by prompt
    # mask:     (B, T) 1 on completion tokens, else 0
    r = rewards.view(-1, group_size)
    advantages = (r - r.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)).view(-1)
    seq_logprobs = (logprobs * mask).sum(dim=1)  # log p_θ(y)
    return -(advantages * seq_logprobs).mean()

The advantages are constants that carry no gradient, so differentiating this loss gives exactly the estimator from the previous sections, with advantages in place of rewards.Many implementations instead divide the summed loss by the total number of completion tokens in the batch. That changes more than the scale: the denominator varies with the sampled lengths, so it reweights completions by length. Dr. GRPO discusses this bias. PPO, GRPO, DAPO, and most other RL algorithms used for LLMs start from this loss and add clipping, masking, or reweighting.

The on-policy assumption

Both identities in this post, the log-derivative rewrite and the zero-mean score, assume that the completions are sampled from the same distribution pθp_\thetapθ​ that we differentiate. In the rewrite, pθp_\thetapθ​ is both the distribution we average over and the model we differentiate. In the zero-mean identity, averaging over ppp itself is what makes the pushes cancel. If the samples come from even a slightly different distribution, the expected score is no longer guaranteed to be zero, and subtracting a baseline shifts the expected gradient instead of leaving it unchanged.

In practice, this assumption rarely holds exactly. In the reinforce_loss above, logprobs comes from the training framework’s forward pass, but the completions were generated by a separate inference engine, such as vLLM or SGLang. The two are supposed to compute the same distribution, but they seldom do. They can run at different numerical precisions, and in asynchronous setups the inference engine may still be serving weights from a few updates ago. Either way, the completions come from a slightly different model than the one being trained. Part 2 covers what happens when that gap opens up and how to correct for it.

Further reading

  • OpenAI Spinning Up: Intro to Policy Optimization derives the same policy gradient in general RL notation, including the expected grad-log-prob lemma, which is the zero-mean identity above.
  • Lilian Weng’s Policy Gradient Algorithms surveys the family, from REINFORCE through actor-critic methods and PPO.
  • Andrej Karpathy’s Deep Reinforcement Learning: Pong from Pixels builds intuition for policy gradients by training a small network to play Pong.
  • Nathan Lambert’s RLHF book covers policy gradient methods for language models, including PPO, GRPO, and RLOO.

entry.title: NanoGPT Speedrun Worklog
entry.content:
I saw some really awesome GPT-2 speedrun results from people like Keller Jordan, Fern, Braden Koszarsky, and others. I got a little inspired and decided to see how fast I could train GPT-2 on my own hardware.

Technically, the NanoGPT speedrun is to train a neural network to 3.28 validation loss on FineWeb as fast as possible on an 8xH100 node. Keller Jordan maintains a leaderboard here. When I started this experiment on January 16, 2025, the record was 3.14 minutes (!).

I had access to 2× RTX 4090 GPUs, so I followed the same rules on my own hardware. Over six iterations, I reduced the training time from 8.13 hours to 2.55 hours. This worklog records the changes that produced that result; the code and run logs are available in the project repository.

Results

# Description Record time Training Tokens Tokens/Second Date Commit Log
1 Initial baseline 8.13 hours 6.44B 221k 2025/01/16 b3c32f8 here
2.1 Architectural changes 7.51 hours 5.07B 188k 2025/01/18 b7bb93f here
2.2 Muon optimizer 4.53 hours 3.04B 187k 2025/01/23 b91c2c0 here
2.3 Dataloading tweaks 4.26 hours 3.31B 216k 2025/02/18 d59944d here
2.4 Logit Soft-capping at 30 4.01 hours 3.15B 218k 2025/02/23 12eab44 here
3 Longer Sequence Length 2.55 hours 1.88B 205k 2025/03/03 d982ed5 here

1. Initial setup and baseline

Part of the goal of this project was to learn as I went, so I started at the beginning—with Andrej Karpathy’s PyTorch GPT-2 trainer from llm.c. This is the script that Keller Jordan used for his initial baseline. The trainer is very similar to NanoGPT with some minor modifications and simplifications, such as removing dropout.

I upstreamed some QOL improvements and basic tweaks to the training script from Keller’s fork, but did not change any of the core training or modeling logic. Specifically:

  1. Implemented gradient accumulation so that my 2x24GB GPUs simulate the training experience of an 8xH100 machine.
  2. Increased learning rate to 0.0015 and halved the batch size (total batch size is 262144 - that is bs of 32/device * 2 devices * 1024 sequence length * 4 gradient accum steps).
  3. Improved learning rate schedule (linear warmup then linear decay).
  4. Removed all affine scale/bias parameters and switched to RMSNorm.
  5. Padded the vocab size from 50257 to 50304 to make it a multiple of 128 (for better tensor core utilization).
  6. Used PyTorch 2.5.1 (the switch from 2.4 to 2.5 gave ~9% speedup on the 8xH100 leaderboard).

Additionally, I added wandb logging to make it easier to track the training runs.

Commit with the initial setup is here: b3c32f8.

The baseline run time on my 2× RTX 4090 setup was 8.13 hours.

2. Implementing major improvements from the 8xH100 leaderboard

Waiting 8 hours for a result was too slow for effective experimentation, so I began by implementing some of the notable improvements from the 8xH100 leaderboard. I started with the most impactful and easiest changes:

  1. Architectural changes and training tweaks
  2. Muon optimizer
  3. Dataloading tweaks
  4. Logit Softcapping

2.1 Architectural changes and training tweaks

There are some basic architectural changes and modernizations that can be made to the model that will speed up training. These changes are general improvements to the transformer decoder architecture that have been generally adopted since the original GPT-2 paper. The changes are:

  1. RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings). There are many good explanations of RoPE out there so I won’t go into detail here.
  2. ReLU^2 activationReLU^2 activation function. . Many activations that are better than GELU have been proposed since GPT-2. ReLU^2 is a simple one that has been shown to be effective in decreasing training time required to reach a certain validation loss.
  3. No gradient clipping. Gradient clipping can help stabilize training, but it also slows down training. Since this was a speedrun, I removed it. This also eliminated a hyperparameter that needed to be tuned.
  4. Trapezoidal learning rate schedule. While cosine learning rate schedules are the de-facto standard, they can be difficult to work with since changing the number of training steps changes the entire schedule. Trapezoidal learning rate schedules are often easier to reason about / tune around, and they have been shown to match the performance of cosine schedules.

In addition, I tuned the learning rate and batch size.

Once again, many of these changes were downstreamed from the modded-nanogpt repository / 8xH100 speedrun. It wasn’t efficient to reinvent the wheel, and I wanted to reduce training time quickly before doing more targeted experiments.

After implementing these changes (commit b7bb93f), the new run time was 7.51 hours. This run was more data-efficient than the baseline, requiring only 5.07B tokens. However, the tokens/second decreased, likely due to the larger batch size (more gradient accumulation steps tends to translate to lower throughput) and architectural changes such as the inclusion of RoPE. The shorter run time made further experimentation more practical.

2.2 Muon Optimizer

The Muon Optimizer was developed with and for the NanoGPT speedrun by Jordan et al. It is a variant of SGD with Momentum that applies a postprocessing step to the gradient updates to approximately orthogonalize each update matrix. Muon has some connections to approximate second-order optimizersBut are these approximate second-order methods actually second-order? New research suggests that methods like Shampoo and Adam can be viewed as variants of steepest descent under specific norms, and thus are actually first-order methods. like Shampoo.

I highly recommend reading the original Muon blog post for more details, as well as checking out the optimizer comparison for GPT-2 speedrunning that Keller Jordan put together here. For those interested in a more step-by-step walkthrough of Muon, check out this excellent post by Jeremy Bernstein.

Muon is designed to work on Linear layers, so it is not quite a drop-in replacement for AdamW (e.g. it isn’t meant to optimize Embedding layers). However, it can be used to optimize all of the hidden layers of our GPT-2 model. The output lm_head layer and token embeddings were still optimized with AdamW.

Just like on the 8xH100 leaderboard, I observed a massive speedup after switching to Muon. The new run time was 4.53 hours, requiring only 3.04B tokens. The tokens/second remained very similar to the previous run, indicating that the optimizer change did not sacrifice throughput.

2.3 Dataloading Tweaks

The architecture and optimizer changes improved data efficiency, but training throughput dropped from 221k tokens/second to 187k tokens/second—a decrease of roughly 15%. Recovering that throughput offered another path to a shorter run time, so I turned to the dataloading and gradient accumulation logic.

Up to this point, I had loaded a full batch of data on each device and then split it into smaller chunks (micro-batches) for each gradient accumulation step. I changed the logic to load only the next micro-batch and advance the dataloader for each accumulation step.

I also upgraded PyTorch from 2.5 to 2.6, which had recently been released, and removed torch._inductor.config.coordinate_descent_tuning in accordance with the official rules introduced on February 1, 2025.

These tweaks brought throughput back up to 216k tokens/second. To make runs more consistently hit the 3.28 validation loss targetThere is some variance in how long a speedrun candidate takes to reach the target. An official record must attain a mean validation loss below 3.28. I treated this somewhat loosely in the early experiments because the differences between runs were much larger than the observed variance., I also slightly increased the total number of training steps, bringing consumption to 3.31B tokens. The new run time was 4.26 hours, and the changes can be found at d59944d.

At this point, the training time was almost half the baseline.

2.4 Logit Soft-capping

Logit soft-capping is a technique popularized by Gemma 2 and initially used to improve the NanoGPT speedrun by @Grad62304977.

Soft-capping is essentially a smooth and differentiable version of clippingSoft-capping vs Clipping at ±5: : softcap(x, cap)=cap⋅tanh⁡(xcap) \text{softcap(x, cap)} = \text{cap} \cdot \tanh\left(\frac{\text{x}}{\text{cap}}\right) softcap(x, cap)=cap⋅tanh(capx​)

Logit soft-capping prevents logits from growing excessively large by scaling them to a fixed range, which seems to help improve training dynamics. One could argue that this imposes an inductive bias—and in this relatively small-model, low-data regime, that bias appeared to be helpful.

After implementing logit soft-capping with a cap of 30 (and doing some learning-rate tuning), the new run time was 4.01 hours, requiring 3.15B tokens (commit 12eab44). Throughput remained steady at ~218k tokens/second.

3. Longer Training and Evaluation Sequence Length

Up to this point, I had trained and evaluated on sequences of 1024 tokens without being particularly clever about how those sequences were constructed. At each step, the dataloader simply placed the next 1024 tokens into an element of the batch without regard for document boundaries. That meant frequently starting in the middle of a document, cutting it off before its end, and attending to tokens across documents through a simple causal mask.

Cutting off documents in the middle is an especially large issue. See this plot of average loss vs sequence position:

Notice how the first twenty-five or so positions have a much higher average loss than later positions. At the beginning of a sequence, the model has much less context with which to predict the next token. Avoiding needless sequence restarts offered a way to reduce this loss penalty.

A natural question to ask at this point is: how long are sequences in our dataset, on average?

The data revealed that approximately 20% of documents exceeded the 1024-token sequence length. Increasing the sequence length to >=8192 tokens would accommodate virtually all documents in the dataset without truncation.

To address these issues, I made two key changes. First, I extended the sequence length to minimize document splitting across sequence boundaries. Taking this approach to its logical conclusion, I eliminated the traditional batch dimension and effectively used a “batch size” of 1 containing multiple concatenated documents. Second, I added attention masking that prevented cross-document attention while retaining the computational efficiency of sparse attention patterns.

Fortunately, FlexAttention provides an elegant solution that maintains the performance benefits of FlashAttention while enabling these improvements. One of FlexAttention’s primary strengths is its ability to efficiently handle sparse, custom attention masks, making it ideal for our use case.

To implement FlexAttention, I defined a mask that handled the specific requirements of the dataset:

def make_attn_mask(idx, eot_token, window_size=1024):
    # Create a causal mask (only attend to past tokens)
    def causal_mask(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        return q_idx >= kv_idx

    # Track document boundaries using end-of-text tokens
    documents = (idx == eot_token).cumsum(dim=1)

    # Only allow attention within the same document
    def document_mask(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        return documents[b, q_idx] == documents[b, kv_idx]

    # Limit attention to an N-token window for efficiency
    def sliding_window_mask(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        return q_idx - kv_idx <= window_size

    return and_masks(document_mask, causal_mask, sliding_window_mask)

Let’s break down each mask:

  1. Causal Mask: Standard in autoregressive language modeling. Ensures that tokens can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence, preventing information leakage from future tokens.

  2. Document Mask: This restricts attention to tokens within the same document. By tracking document boundaries using end-of-text tokens, we prevent tokens from attending across different documents, which helps the model maintain coherent context within a single document.

  3. Sliding Window Mask: This limits attention to a fixed window of tokens before the current position. This approach balances efficiency with context retention with a clear tradeoff: smaller windows are more efficient but may miss long-range dependencies, while larger windows capture more context at the expense of resources.

The individual component masks are visualized below:

When combined with the and_masks function, these three masksNote that the causal mask is actually redundant to the sliding window mask, as the sliding window mask already ensures that tokens can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence. The causal mask is included here for clarity. work together to create an efficient attention pattern that respects document boundaries, maintains causality, and limits computational overhead for long sequences.

After incorporating FlexAttention with these masks and increasing the sequence length to 32768 tokens, I observed another massive speedupThis speedup is a bit of a hack against the target metric. Supporting longer sequences is a straightforward way to drop the loss on the validation set, but is unlikely to provide a meaningful improvement to the overall performance of the model on practical benchmarks.. The final run time was 2.55 hours, requiring only 1.88B tokens—a large data-efficiency improvement. Throughput dropped slightly to ~205k tokens/second. See commit d982ed5 for the full details.

Summary

The final 2.55-hour run was 3.2x faster than the 8.13-hour baseline and used 1.88B training tokens instead of 6.44B. Muon produced the largest improvement that was independent of the evaluation setup. The final reduction came from longer, document-aware sequences and was more specific to the validation-loss target.

This post records the completed 2025 round of experiments, with 2.55 hours as the last measured result. I may revisit the speedrun in the future, either on the same GPUs or on different hardware. The numbers here are specific to the two-RTX-4090 setup and are not directly comparable to the 8xH100 leaderboard times.
